entry.title: Four ways New York could make a first home cheaper to buy
entry.summary: The city's housing shortage will take years to fix. Its tax on mortgages, the cliffs in its transfer tax and gaps in its sales data could change much sooner.

entry.title: A $1.6 million sale that stayed in the family
entry.summary: The city's sales file shows a $1,625,000 house sale. The form filed with the deed says the house passed between relatives, and one of the sellers was the buyer. Such forms are common, and the open data leaves their answers out.

entry.title: Same $900,000 condo, $13,860 more in tax for the buyer with a mortgage
entry.summary: Buyers who borrow owe a recording tax on the loan that cash buyers never pay. Across four boroughs it comes to about $244 million a year.

entry.title: One dollar over $2 million costs a New York buyer $5,000 in tax
entry.summary: Since the 2019 tax change, sales at exactly $1,999,999 went from about one a year to about 21. Most deals that would have closed at $2 million now close just below it, and four in ten still pay the jump.

entry.title: Half the cash-buyer discount fades once possible family sales are set aside
entry.summary: In New York City records, houses bought for cash sell for about 9% less. Set aside sales between people who share a surname and the gap halves; when a company pays cash, it is too small to tell from zero.

entry.title: When a lender takes back a home, the record can look like a sale
entry.summary: Foreclosure deeds can carry a lender’s bid or a cancelled debt, and most reach the city’s sales file as if they were prices. In the Bronx, counting them shifts the 2010 house-price index by about a tenth.

entry.title: Correction: condominium links are being rechecked
entry.summary: An incorrect lot-number limit in my code excluded valid candidate units. The earlier Bronx coverage gap should not be interpreted as missing public records.
